title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
text:
Part 3 showed a conflict between two people sharing main. This one is the version you will actually meet if your group follows the pull-request discipline, and it looks different enough to be worth its own walkthrough.
Everything below is real output from PR #2 of the example repository.
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
text:
How you get here
Nobody did anything wrong. That is the point.

You branch off main and start writing.
While you are working, a teammate’s pull request is merged. main has moved on.
Their change touched the same lines yours did.

Your branch is now based on a version of the project that no longer exists.
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
section: Your push still works — and that is the trap
text:
Your push still works — and that is the trap
git push -u origin feature/limitations
 * [new branch]      feature/limitations -> feature/limitations
branch 'feature/limitations' set up to track 'origin/feature/limitations'
No rejection, no warning. Branches never conflict on push, because nobody else is pushing to your branch. This is the opposite of Part 3, where the push itself was rejected.
So you open the pull request happily:
gh pr create --base main --title "Note that the simulation guarantees correct specification"
https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic/pull/2
And then GitHub tells you.
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
section: Finding out: ask, do not guess
text:
Finding out: ask, do not guess
On the PR page, the green merge button is replaced by a warning that the branch has conflicts which must be resolved. From the terminal:
gh pr view 2 --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus
PR #2  feature/limitations -> main
  mergeable        : CONFLICTING
  mergeStateStatus : DIRTY






UNKNOWN just means “ask again in a moment”



GitHub works out mergeability in the background. Immediately after a push you will often get:
mergeable: UNKNOWN   state: UNKNOWN
That is not a problem. Wait a few seconds and ask again.








Say this to Claude Code




My pull request says it has conflicts. What conflicts, and what do I need to decide?
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
section: The fix: bring main into your branch
text:
The fix: bring main into your branch
The direction matters, and it is the one thing to get right on this page.
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main       # main comes INTO your branch
Auto-merging report.qmd
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in report.qmd
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.






Why this direction and not the other



You could in principle merge your branch into main locally and push that. Do not. It would put your unfinished, unreviewed work onto main directly, bypassing the pull request and the teammate who was supposed to read it.
Resolve inside your own branch. main stays untouched until somebody merges your PR. Your branch is your problem; main is the group’s.
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
section: Reading this conflict: the sides are not equal
text:
Reading this conflict: the sides are not equal





flowchart LR
    M1["main<br/>when you branched"] --> M2["main<br/>now"]
    M1 --> B1["your branch"]
    M2 -->|"git merge origin/main"| R["resolve<br/>here"]
    B1 --> R
    R -->|"git push"| PR["PR becomes<br/>MERGEABLE"]






The real conflict from PR #2:
<<<<<<< HEAD
This is a demonstration of the estimator on synthetic data. It is not
evidence about any real intervention.

A further limitation: the simulation assumes the arm effect is constant
across ages, so the model is correctly specified by construction. Real
data would not be so obliging.
=======
These data are synthetic. Nothing above is evidence about any real
intervention, and the numbers should not be quoted outside this course.
>>>>>>> origin/main
Now notice something that was not true in Part 3:

HEAD is your branch — work nobody has reviewed yet
below ======= is main — work the group has already accepted







Default to keeping main’s decision, and adding yours



In Part 3 both sides were equally provisional, so combining them was a free choice. Here they are not. Somebody wrote that disclaimer, somebody else reviewed it, and it was merged. Overwriting it with your own phrasing quietly reverses a decision your group already made — and because it arrives inside a conflict resolution, nobody will see it in review.
So the resolution kept main’s wording and added the separate point:
These data are synthetic. Nothing above is evidence about any real
intervention, and the numbers should not be quoted outside this course.

A further limitation: the simulation assumes the arm effect is constant
across ages, so the model is correctly specified by construction. Real
data would not be so obliging.
If you genuinely think main is wrong, that is a conversation in the pull request, not a silent edit inside a merge.
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
text:
The two checks, again
grep -nE '^(<<<<<<<|=======|>>>>>>>)' report.qmd || echo "clean"
quarto render report.qmd
clean
Output created: report.html
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
section: Commit and push — to your branch
text:
Commit and push — to your branch
git add report.qmd
git commit -m "Merge main into feature/limitations"
git push
Plain git push, because you are still on your branch and it is already tracking origin. You are not pushing to main.
Ask GitHub again:
gh pr view 2 --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus
mergeable: MERGEABLE   state: CLEAN
The pull request updated itself. Your teammate can now review it and press Squash and merge.
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
text:
The web “Resolve conflicts” button
GitHub offers to resolve simple conflicts in the browser. It works, and for a one-line README clash it is fine.






But it cannot run your code



Resolving in the browser means you commit a file you have never rendered or sourced. That is exactly how <<<<<<< HEAD reaches a submitted report, and how a half-merged R script gets onto main.
For anything that has to execute — .R, .qmd, .Rmd — resolve locally and render before you push.
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts
section: Part 3 vs Part 3½, side by side
text:
Part 3 vs Part 3½, side by side









Part 3: shared main
Part 3½: pull request




Who collided
two people on main
your branch vs merged work


First symptom
push rejected
push succeeds; PR says CONFLICTING


Where you find out
terminal, immediately
GitHub, after you open the PR


Command that surfaces it
git pull
git merge origin/main


Sides in the conflict
two drafts, equal standing
your draft vs accepted work


Default resolution
combine both
keep main, add yours


What you push afterwards
main
your branch



Same mechanism underneath: two changes to the same lines, and a human decides. Only the moment of discovery differs.
crumbs: Part 3½ — When the pull request conflicts

title: Instructor notes
text: Not for students. Keep this page out of the handout you hand out, or delete it from _quarto.yml before publishing.

title: Instructor notes
text:
Timing








Part
Format
Time




0 · Setup
homework, before class
20 min


1 · Four ideas
lecture + napkin check
15 min


2 · Solo walkthrough
live demo, then they do it
40 min


3 · Collaboration cycle
in groups, one PR each
45 min


3 · Conflict, on purpose
scripted, whole class together
30 min


3½ · Conflict on a pull request
scripted, in pairs
20 min


4–5 · Troubleshooting, rules
read + discuss
15 min



Two sessions of 90 minutes, or one long workshop. Part 0 as homework is not optional — doing installs and OAuth in class will consume the entire session and half the students will still be stuck.

title: Instructor notes
text:
Check before the session
Ask every student to paste the output of these four commands into the course forum a few days before:
git --version
gh auth status
git config --global --list | grep -E "user\.|defaultBranch|rebase"
R --version
The failure you will see most is a missing pull.rebase. It does not break anything until two people diverge — that is, precisely during the group exercise — and then it fails hard with a wall of hints. Catch it early.

title: Instructor notes
text:
Running the conflict exercise
Do not hope a conflict happens. Script it:

Pair the students. Both pull main.
Both open report.qmd and write a paragraph in the Interpretation section — the same lines, their own words.
Student C pushes first. Fine.
Student A pushes. Rejected. Stop here and read the hint together as a class — this is the single most valuable 60 seconds of the session.
Student A pulls → conflict.
Resolve by hand first, so everyone has seen the markers in a real file.
Then re-run it and resolve with a prompt, so they see the difference.

The pedagogical payload is step 4, not step 5. The rejected push is the moment they understand that git is protecting the other person.

title: Instructor notes
text:
Running the Part 3½ exercise
Do this after Part 3, because the contrast is the lesson: in Part 3 the push is rejected, here it succeeds and GitHub complains later. Students who only see one of the two conclude the wrong general rule.
To engineer it reliably, in pairs:

Both pull main.
Student A branches (feature/limitations) and edits the closing lines of the Interpretation section. Does not push yet.
Student C edits the same lines and gets them onto main — in class, pushing straight to main is the quickest way; in their real project this happens because C’s PR was merged.
A pushes the branch — it succeeds. Pause here and ask the class whether everything is fine. Most will say yes.
A opens the PR. gh pr view <n> --json mergeable,mergeStateStatus → CONFLICTING / DIRTY.
A fixes it with git merge origin/main inside the branch, resolves, renders, pushes. The PR flips to MERGEABLE / CLEAN.

Two points worth labouring:

Direction. Merging their branch into main locally would “work” and would bypass review entirely. Ask them why that is bad before you tell them.
Asymmetry. Here HEAD is their unreviewed branch and the other side is merged, accepted work. The Part 3 instinct of “combine both equally” can silently reverse a group decision inside a merge commit, where no reviewer will ever see it.

mergeable: UNKNOWN right after a push is normal — GitHub computes it asynchronously. Tell them in advance or you will field the question five times.

title: Instructor notes
section: Why the example project is shaped this way
text:
Why the example project is shaped this way
Owner-per-file plus one shared section. Their real group work should flow without conflicts; the shared Interpretation section is the designated safe place to learn the skill.
Simulated data with a known effect (arm effect = −4). The model recovers −5.23 (95% CI −7.53 to −2.94). The interval covers the truth and the point estimate misses it by 1.2. Almost no real dataset lets students see sampling variation against a known answer, so this is worth a detour even though the course is about git. It also makes the conflict resolution substantive: the two paragraphs disagree about what to emphasise, not about facts.
The 4 KB CSV is committed on purpose. “Never commit data” is the usual advice and it is wrong often enough to be harmful — students who follow it literally produce repositories nobody can run. Teach the criterion (small · synthetic or public · needed to run the code) rather than the slogan.

title: Instructor notes
section: The example repo uses merge commits on purpose
text:
The example repo uses merge commits on purpose
The handout tells students to Squash and merge. The example repository itself uses merge commits, and Part 3 now has a collapsed note explaining why: squashing would flatten away the branch topology that the repository exists to demonstrate.
Do not “fix” this later. If you ever rebuild the example repo, keep merge commits, and keep recommending squash for student projects. The two-sentence version for class: squashing makes history readable, which is what you want; it also makes branching invisible, which is what we need to look at today.
The graph is worth putting on a slide as-is. Read bottom to top it contains a clean PR, a shared-branch conflict, a stale PR, and a conflict resolved inside a branch — all four situations students will meet, in one picture.

title: Instructor notes
text:
Things students reliably get wrong








Mistake
Why it happens
Pre-empt it by




Not pulling before working
Nothing visibly breaks until it does
Making “look at the Git pane arrows” a ritual


Forgetting local main after a merge
GitHub shows merged; their laptop doesn’t move
Showing git branch -vv before and after


Committing .RData / rendered HTML
RStudio creates them silently
.gitignore before the first commit


Project inside Dropbox/OneDrive
It is where their coursework already lives
Saying it out loud in Part 2, with the reason


--force after a rejected push
It is the top Stack Overflow answer
Naming it explicitly as forbidden, and why


Merging their own PR
It is one click
Grading it

title: Instructor notes
section: On letting AI do the git work
text:
On letting AI do the git work
The design assumption is that students delegate mechanics and own meaning. It holds up as long as they have the model from Part 1. Without it, an AI-driven student will resolve a conflict by accepting whichever version the model liked, and never notice that a teammate’s paragraph vanished.
So the napkin check is the real gate, not the walkthrough. If a student cannot draw the four places, more practice with prompts will not help them.

title: Instructor notes
text:
Assessment suggestions
Grade the repository, not just the report:

Process (visible in the history) — commits small and frequent; messages explain why; every contribution merged via a PR someone else approved; main renders from a fresh clone.
Hygiene — no data over ~1 MB, no secrets, .gitignore present from the first commit.
Contribution — git shortlog -sn shows who committed what. Useful for detecting the group where one person did everything; do not use it mechanically, since pair programming and reviewing are real work that shows up as few commits.

A good single exam question: “Your teammate pushed work you don’t have, and your push was rejected. Explain what happened and what you will do — and what would happen if you used --force.”

title: Instructor notes
section: The Dropbox warning is not theoretical
text:
The Dropbox warning is not theoretical
While these pages were being written — inside a Dropbox folder — Dropbox created 18 “conflicted copy” files in the render output and replaced _site/index.html with a 253-byte redirect stub. The site silently served a broken page with every stylesheet and script 404ing.
Nothing was lost, because the corruption hit only the disposable _site/ output and not the .qmd sources. But it is a clean demonstration of the point Part 2 makes to students: a sync client and a build tool both writing to the same directory will eventually collide.
Two fixes, in order of preference:

Keep projects out of synced folders. ~/projects, not Dropbox.
If a project must live in Dropbox, mark the build output as Dropbox-ignored before rendering:

mkdir -p _site .quarto
xattr -w com.dropbox.ignored 1 _site
xattr -w com.dropbox.ignored 1 .quarto
Applied to the old Dropbox copy, this took the conflicted-copy count from 18 to zero across three consecutive renders. It did not eliminate the problem entirely — one further render still failed with
ERROR: NotFound: No such file or directory (os error 2): rename ...
which succeeded on a plain retry. So treat it as a mitigation that makes a folder usable, not a cure. It protects the output directory only; it does nothing for a .git directory. Do not rely on it to make a git repository safe inside Dropbox.
In the end this tutorial and its example project were both moved out to ~/projects/, which is what Part 2 tells students to do. Three renders in the new location: no errors, no conflicted copies. If you are going to ask students to keep projects out of synced folders, the course materials should not be sitting in one.

title: Instructor notes
text:
Maintaining this tutorial
Every command and output in these pages was executed on macOS with git 2.39.3, gh 2.90.0, R 4.6.0 and Quarto 1.4.554. The Windows and Linux install instructions were not tested — verify them once on a student machine before first use.
Re-render after editing:
quarto render

title: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub
text:
One member of the group does this once, while the others watch. Then everyone does it again alone, with a throwaway project, because you only learn it by doing it.
Every command on this page has been run for real; the outputs shown are the actual outputs.
crumbs: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub

title: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub
text:
1. Make an RStudio Project
In RStudio: File → New Project → New Directory → New Project.

Directory name: penguin-clinic
Create as a subdirectory of: somewhere sensible, e.g. ~/projects
Leave “Create a git repository” unchecked — we will do it deliberately







Do not put your project in Dropbox, OneDrive or iCloud



A sync client and git both want to manage the same files, and the sync client can corrupt git’s internal bookkeeping by writing into .git at the wrong moment. More importantly: GitHub is now your sharing mechanism. Putting a git project in a sync folder is doing the same job twice, badly.
Use ~/projects/ or Documents/projects/ — anywhere that is not synced.


Why a Project and not just a folder? Because .Rproj fixes your working directory. Every path in your code becomes relative to the project root, so read.csv("data/clinic_visits.csv") works on your teammate’s laptop too. This is a precondition for collaboration, not a nicety.
crumbs: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub

title: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub
section: 2. Open the project folder in Claude Code
text:
2. Open the project folder in Claude Code
Open Claude Code and point it at the project folder you just made. It needs to be in the project, otherwise it will put files in the wrong place.
crumbs: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub

title: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub
text:
3. Build the project skeleton






Say this to Claude Code




Set up this R project for group work: an R/ folder with three analysis scripts, a data-raw/ script that simulates a small dataset, a data/ folder, and a report.qmd that sources the scripts. Also write a README saying who owns which file.



The structure we are aiming at:
penguin-clinic/
├── penguin-clinic.Rproj
├── README.md
├── .gitignore
├── data-raw/00-simulate-data.R   # makes the data, so provenance is in the repo
├── data/clinic_visits.csv        # 4 KB, simulated
├── R/01-clean.R                  # student A owns
├── R/02-describe.R               # student B owns
├── R/03-model.R                  # student C owns
└── report.qmd                    # shared; conflicts live here
Check it works before going near git. A broken project in version control is still broken.
Rscript -e 'source("R/01-clean.R"); print(nrow(load_visits()))'
crumbs: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub

title: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub
section: 4. Start the repository and write a .gitignore
text:
4. Start the repository and write a .gitignore






Say this to Claude Code




Make this a git repository with main as the default branch, and write a .gitignore suitable for an R and Quarto project. Keep the small simulated CSV in version control but exclude RStudio session state, rendered output and anything that looks like a secret.



git init -b main
The .gitignore is the one file worth understanding, because the mistakes it prevents are the expensive ones:
# RStudio session junk — machine-specific, never useful to anyone else
.Rproj.user/
.Rhistory
.RData

# secrets: NEVER commit these
.Renviron
.env

# rendered output — commit the source, not the result
report.html
report_files/
/_site/
/.quarto/

# OS noise
.DS_Store






“Never commit data” is wrong advice



You will hear it anyway. The real criterion is:







Commit it
Do not commit it




Small (< ~1 MB)
Large — git stores every version forever


Simulated or public
Personal, identifiable, or under a data agreement


Needed to run the code
Re-derivable from something else in the repo



Our 4 KB simulated CSV is committed on purpose: without it, nobody can run your code. A real patient export would be excluded, and the README would say where to get it.
And the hard part: git never forgets. If you commit a file with patient data or an API key and then delete it, it is still in the history and still on GitHub. Removing it properly is difficult and you must assume the secret is burned. So get .gitignore right before the first commit.
crumbs: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub

title: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub
text:
5. First commit






Say this to Claude Code




Show me what would be committed, then commit it with a message explaining what this project is.



git status --short          # ?? means untracked
git add -A
git status --short          # A  means staged
git commit -m "Set up project skeleton for the group analysis"
Confirm the .gitignore actually worked:
git status --ignored --short | grep '^!!'
Real output from this project:
!! report.html
!! report_files/
That is .gitignore doing its job. If you see !! data/patient_export.csv, good. If you see it staged with A, stop and fix it.
crumbs: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub

title: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub
section: 6. Create the GitHub repository and push
text:
6. Create the GitHub repository and push






Say this to Claude Code




Create a public GitHub repository called penguin-clinic from this folder and push main to it.



gh repo create penguin-clinic --public --source=. --remote=origin --push
Real output:
https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic
To https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic.git
 * [new branch]      HEAD -> main
branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.
That one command did three things worth naming:

created the repository on GitHub
added it to your local repo under the name origin — that word just means “the GitHub copy”
pushed main and set it to track origin/main, so from now on plain git push and git pull know where to go

Open the URL. Your files are there. Check that the ignored ones are not.
crumbs: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub

title: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub
section: 7. The loop you will now repeat forever
text:
7. The loop you will now repeat forever
Change something in RStudio → commit → push → refresh the browser.






Say this to Claude Code




Commit and push this change, with a message explaining why I did it.



Watch RStudio’s Git pane (top right, appears after you reopen the project) while you do it. It is the window through which you see the four places from Part 1:

files appear with ? when untracked, M when modified
checkboxes are the staging area
Commit moves them into your local history
the ↑ / ↓ arrows show how many commits you are ahead of / behind GitHub







Look at the arrows every time you sit down



↓ 2 means your teammates have pushed twice and you do not have their work yet. Pull before you start. That one habit prevents most conflicts.
crumbs: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub

title: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub
text:
8. Add your teammates
On GitHub: Settings → Collaborators → Add people. They need to accept the invitation by email before they can push.
gh repo view --web    # opens the repo in your browser
crumbs: Part 2 — One person, one project, on GitHub

title: Part 3 — Working as a group
text: This is the part that actually matters. Everything before it was single-player.

title: Part 3 — Working as a group
text:
1. Everyone else joins: clone
Each other group member does this once.






Say this to Claude Code




Clone github.com/OUR-GROUP/penguin-clinic into my projects folder.



cd ~/projects
git clone https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic.git
Then open penguin-clinic.Rproj in RStudio. You have a complete copy: every file, and the entire history. A clone already knows where it came from, so git push and git pull work immediately with no setup.






Clone once, pull forever



Cloning again because “it stopped working” is the student equivalent of reinstalling Windows. You almost never need to.

title: Part 3 — Working as a group
text:
2. The contribution cycle
This is the loop for every piece of work, all term. Five steps.





flowchart TD
    P["<b>1. pull</b><br/>get everyone's latest work"] --> B["<b>2. branch</b><br/>start your own line of work"]
    B --> C["<b>3. commit</b><br/>as often as you like, locally"]
    C --> PR["<b>4. push + open a Pull Request</b><br/>ask your group to take your work"]
    PR --> M["<b>5. a teammate merges,<br/>then everyone pulls</b>"]
    M --> P







Step 1 & 2 — pull, then branch
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c feature/describe-by-sex
Branch names: feature/what-it-does. Not ulo, not new, not test2. Someone reading the pull request list in three weeks should know what each one was for.


Step 3 — work, and commit as you go






Say this to Claude Code




Commit what I’ve done so far with a message about adding the sex-stratified summary table.



Commit often and small. Every commit is a point you can return to. A single commit called “did the whole analysis” is a point you can return to only if you want to lose the whole analysis.
Check your code runs before you commit. In this project:
Rscript -e 'source("R/01-clean.R"); source("R/02-describe.R"); print(describe_by_sex(load_visits()))'
Real output:
        arm sex  n mean_score sd_score
1   control   F 26      60.32     6.06
2 treatment   F 25      56.08     6.02
3   control   M 34      60.77     6.33
4 treatment   M 35      54.76     7.67


Step 4 — push the branch and open a Pull Request






Say this to Claude Code




Push this branch and open a pull request explaining what I changed, why, and how a reviewer can check it.



git push -u origin feature/describe-by-sex
gh pr create --base main --title "Add sex-stratified descriptives" --body "..."
A pull request worth reviewing answers three questions. Ours did:

What — Adds describe_by_sex() in R/02-describe.R and shows the table in the Descriptives section.
Why — The arms were balanced by construction (60/60) but sex was not, so the pooled table could hide a difference between strata.
How to check this — describe_by_sex(load_visits()); expect 4 rows summing to n = 120.

That third heading is the one students skip and reviewers need most.


Step 5 — a teammate reviews and merges






You do not merge your own pull request



Someone else in the group opens it on GitHub, reads the diff, and presses Merge pull request → Squash and merge.
Choose Squash and merge, not the default “Create a merge commit”: it puts exactly one commit on main per contribution, which makes main’s history readable and makes undoing a bad contribution a single step.








Why the example repository does not follow its own advice





If you look at the history of the example repository, you will find merge commits, not squashes. That is deliberate.
Squashing hides the branching. For your project that is exactly what you want — a clean line of contributions on main. But for a repository whose job is to teach branching, throwing the branches away would throw away the lesson. Merge commits keep the shape visible:
*   76e5a30 Merge pull request #2
|\
| *   e9868fb Merge main into feature/limitations
| |\
|/|
* | 76c6037 Strengthen the synthetic-data disclaimer
| * b41c5d3 Note that the simulation guarantees correct specification
|/
*   929bf6e Merge student C's interpretation
|\
| * de43b31 Write the Interpretation section
* | b10d837 Add interpretation with estimate and CI
|/
*   32afb9c Merge pull request #1
|\
| * 26826f2 Add sex-stratified descriptives
|/
* 752e171 Set up project skeleton
Read from the bottom, that is every situation in this tutorial: a clean pull request (#1), a conflict between two people sharing main (929bf6e), a pull request that went stale because main moved on (76c6037 vs b41c5d3), and that conflict resolved inside the branch (e9868fb) before it was merged (#2).
Try it yourself:
git clone https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic.git
cd penguin-clinic
git log --oneline --graph
So: squash in your own project, and read the example’s graph to understand what squashing would have hidden.





The step everyone forgets
Merging on GitHub does not change anything on your laptop. Your local main is now behind. Real output from this project immediately after the merge:
* feature/describe-by-sex 26826f2 [origin/feature/describe-by-sex] Add sex-...
  main                    752e171 [origin/main] Set up project skeleton
Local main still points at the old commit. So after every merge, everyone in the group runs:






Say this to Claude Code




My PR was merged. Update my main and clean up the branch.



git switch main
git pull
git fetch --prune                        # forget branches deleted on GitHub
git branch -d feature/describe-by-sex    # delete the local copy
Skip this and you will, a week later, commit new work onto a branch that was merged and deleted, and be very confused.

title: Part 3 — Working as a group
text:
3. The merge conflict, on purpose
Now the thing you are actually here for. Do this deliberately, in class, while nothing is at stake.
Setup. Two group members both edit the Interpretation section of report.qmd — the same lines — without pulling in between.

What happens: student C pushes first
git commit -am "Write the Interpretation section"
git push
Fine. GitHub now has student C’s paragraph.


Student A, who did not pull, tries to push
git commit -am "Add interpretation with effect estimate and CI"
git push
Real output:
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/...'
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally. This is usually caused by another repository pushing
hint: to the same ref. You may want to first integrate the remote changes
hint: (e.g., 'git pull ...') before pushing again.






Read that hint. It is telling you the truth.



“The remote contains work that you do not have locally” means: your teammate pushed something and you would be overwriting it. Git is refusing to let you destroy their work.
There is a way to force it — git push --force — and it does exactly what it sounds like: it deletes your teammate’s commits from GitHub. Never type it. If some website tells you to, that website is not thinking about your group.




So student A pulls
git pull
Real output:
Auto-merging report.qmd
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in report.qmd
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
git status tells you precisely what git wants:
You have unmerged paths.
  (fix conflicts and run "git commit")
  (use "git merge --abort" to abort the merge)

Unmerged paths:
    both modified:   report.qmd






git merge --abort is your safety net



It puts everything back exactly as it was before the pull. If you panic, use it. Nothing is lost. Then try again when you are calm.




Reading the conflict
Open report.qmd in RStudio. It contains both versions:
<<<<<<< HEAD
Treatment was associated with a lower score than control (adjusted
difference -5.23, 95% CI -7.53 to -2.94). We stress that these data are
simulated, so this is a demonstration of the estimator and not evidence
about any real intervention.
=======
In this simulated dataset the treatment arm scored about 5 points lower
than control after adjustment for age and sex. Because the data were
generated with a known arm effect of -4, the estimate is close to the
truth but not identical - ordinary sampling variation.
>>>>>>> de43b31

<<<<<<< HEAD up to ======= — your version
======= down to >>>>>>> — their version
de43b31 — the ID of their commit



Resolving it: the actual skill
Look at those two paragraphs. Student A has the numbers. Student C has the comparison against the known simulated effect. Neither is wrong, and each says something the other omitted. So the resolution keeps both:
Treatment was associated with a lower score than control (adjusted
difference -5.23 points, 95% CI -7.53 to -2.94). These data were simulated
with a known arm effect of -4, so the estimate is close to the truth but not
identical: the interval covers -4, and the gap between -5.23 and -4 is
ordinary sampling variation rather than bias.

This is a demonstration of the estimator on synthetic data. It is not
evidence about any real intervention.






This is why you cannot fully delegate this



Ask Claude to resolve a conflict and it will produce something clean and plausible. It may quietly pick one version, or blend them into a sentence your group never agreed to claim. It does not know which number you decided to report, or that you agreed last week to always flag the data as simulated.
Delegate the mechanics, own the meaning. A good prompt tells it the decision:

There’s a conflict in the Interpretation section. Keep both points: my estimate with its confidence interval, and C’s comparison against the known simulated effect of -4. Merge them into one paragraph and keep the sentence saying the data are synthetic.





Before you commit the resolution — two checks

All markers gone?

grep -nE '^(<<<<<<<|=======|>>>>>>>)' report.qmd || echo "clean"

Does it still run? A half-resolved file is valid text and invalid code.

quarto render report.qmd
Skipping check 2 is how <<<<<<< HEAD ends up in a submitted report.


Finish the merge
git add report.qmd
git commit -m "Merge student C's interpretation with the effect estimate"
git push
The history now shows exactly what happened:
*   929bf6e Merge student C's interpretation with the effect estimate
|\
| * de43b31 Write the Interpretation section        <- student C
* | b10d837 Add interpretation with estimate and CI <- student A
|/
*   32afb9c Merge pull request #1
Both people’s work survives, and the record shows who wrote what and how it was reconciled. That is the entire value proposition of git in one picture.


And the other members pull
git pull
Updating de43b31..929bf6e
Fast-forward
 report.qmd | 12 ++++++++----
“Fast-forward” means there was nothing to reconcile — you simply moved forward. Most pulls look like this. Conflicts are the exception, not the rule.

title: Part 3 — Working as a group
section: 4. How to almost never have conflicts
text:
4. How to almost never have conflicts
Conflicts need two people editing the same lines between pulls. Break any link in that chain:

Own your files. The README says who owns what. Stay in your file.
Pull before you start. Push when you stop. Shrinks the window.
Small, frequent pull requests. A branch alive for two weeks is a conflict with a countdown.
In shared prose, one paragraph per person, on its own lines. Conflicts are line-based, so blank lines between contributions genuinely help.
Say out loud when you are about to touch a shared file. The cheapest version-control tool is a group chat message.

title: Part 3 — Working as a group
section: Next: the other kind of conflict
text:
Next: the other kind of conflict
The conflict above happened because two people shared main. If your group follows the pull-request discipline, you will more often meet a conflict that shows up on the pull request instead — your push succeeds, and GitHub tells you afterwards. That is Part 3½, and the correct fix points in the opposite direction.

title: Part 4 — When it breaks
text:
Say this to Claude Code




Something’s wrong with git. Here’s the whole error: [paste everything]. What’s the state of my repository and what should I do?



Paste the entire message, hints included. Git’s hints usually contain the answer, and students habitually paste only the first red line.
Before anything else, two harmless commands that tell you where you are:
git status
git log --oneline --graph -10
Nothing in this world is lost as long as you committed it. Git’s default behaviour is to refuse to destroy work; almost every alarming message is git protecting you.

title: Part 4 — When it breaks
text:
Say this to Claude Code




Something’s wrong with git. Here’s the whole error: [paste everything]. What’s the state of my repository and what should I do?



Paste the entire message, hints included. Git’s hints usually contain the answer, and students habitually paste only the first red line.
Before anything else, two harmless commands that tell you where you are:
git status
git log --oneline --graph -10
Nothing in this world is lost as long as you committed it. Git’s default behaviour is to refuse to destroy work; almost every alarming message is git protecting you.

title: Part 4 — When it breaks
section: The five errors you will actually meet
text:
The five errors you will actually meet
All five outputs below are real, captured from the worked example.

1. Rejected push
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally.
What it means — a teammate pushed; you would be overwriting them.
Fix — git pull, resolve anything that conflicts, then git push.
Never — git push --force. That deletes your teammate’s commits from GitHub.


2. Need to specify how to reconcile
fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches.
What it means — you and GitHub both have new commits, and git has not been told whether to merge or rebase. Not your fault: a missing setting.
Fix — the Part 0 line you skipped:
git config --global pull.rebase false
git pull


3. Merge conflict
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in report.qmd
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
What it means — the same lines changed on both sides. Working as designed.
Fix — see Part 3. Or escape with git merge --abort, which puts everything back untouched.


3b. Your pull request says CONFLICTING
mergeable        : CONFLICTING
mergeStateStatus : DIRTY
What it means — your branch was fine when you made it, but main moved on underneath you and touched the same lines. Your push was never rejected, so this is the first you hear of it.
Fix — bring main into your branch, not the other way round:
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
# resolve, check it renders, then:
git push
The PR updates itself. Full walkthrough in Part 3½.
Watch out — in this conflict the other side is work your group has already reviewed and merged. Default to keeping it and adding yours.


4. Author identity unknown
*** Please tell me who you are.
Run
  git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
  git config --global user.name "Your Name"
fatal: empty ident name (for <>) not allowed
What it means — git will not stamp a commit with nobody’s name.
Fix — run the two lines it gives you. Use the email your GitHub account uses, or GitHub will not link the commits to you.


5. You committed something huge or secret
Not one error message but several — a push that hangs for minutes, or GitHub refusing a file over 100 MB.
Fix — if you have not pushed yet, this is easy:






Say this to Claude Code




I accidentally committed data/huge_export.csv in my last commit and haven’t pushed. Undo that commit, keep my other changes, and add the file to .gitignore.



If you have already pushed a secret, the situation is different and you should tell your instructor. Rewriting shared history is disruptive, and — the important part — assume the secret is already compromised. Revoke the API key, change the password. Removing it from the repository does not un-publish it.

title: Part 4 — When it breaks
text:
Prompt cheat-sheet
Say these instead of learning commands.

Every day







What you want
Say




Start work
“Pull the latest changes and tell me what my teammates changed.”


Save progress
“Commit my work with a message explaining why I made this change.”


Publish it
“Push this to GitHub.”


Start a task
“Make a branch for adding the age-adjusted model.”


Submit it
“Push this branch and open a pull request explaining what and why.”


After it’s merged
“My PR was merged — update my main and delete the old branch.”





Finding out what is going on







What you want
Say




Where am I?
“What branch am I on, and is anything uncommitted?”


What changed?
“Show me what I’ve changed since my last commit.”


Who did this?
“Who last changed the model in R/03-model.R, and what was the message?”


Recent history
“Summarise what the group has done in the last week.”


Am I behind?
“Am I behind GitHub? What would I get if I pulled?”





Fixing things







What you want
Say




Undo uncommitted mess
“Throw away my uncommitted changes to R/02-describe.R.”


Undo last commit, keep work
“Undo my last commit but keep the changes in my files.”


Undo a merged contribution
“Revert the commit that added the sex-stratified table.”


Go back and look
“Show me report.qmd as it was three commits ago.”


Wrong branch
“I did this work on main by mistake. Move it to a new branch.”









Two prompts to be careful with



“Throw away my changes” and “undo my last commit” can destroy work that was never committed, which is the one kind git cannot recover.
Before agreeing to anything that discards work, ask: “what exactly will be lost?” A good answer names files. If you are unsure, commit first — a commit you do not want is easy to discard later; uncommitted work you deleted is gone.

title: Part 4 — When it breaks
text:
What not to delegate







Delegate freely
Decide yourself




Writing commit messages
Whether your code is correct


add/commit/push/pull/branches
Which version of a conflict is right


Writing .gitignore
Whether a data file may be published at all


Opening pull requests
Whether a teammate’s PR should be merged


Explaining an error
Whether to force-push (answer: no)



The pattern: anything reversible and mechanical, delegate. Anything about meaning or about publishing, own.

title: Part 1 — The four ideas
text: No computers for this part. Ten minutes, and then you are allowed to let the AI do the typing for the rest of your life.

title: Part 1 — The four ideas
text:
Idea 1: four places, three moves
Your work exists in four places. Git’s commands are just moves between them.





flowchart LR
    A["<b>Working directory</b><br/>the files you edit<br/>in RStudio"]
    B["<b>Staging area</b><br/>what will go into<br/>the next snapshot"]
    C["<b>Local repository</b><br/>your history<br/>on your laptop"]
    D[("<b>GitHub</b><br/>the shared history<br/>everyone sees")]

    A -->|"git add"| B
    B -->|"git commit"| C
    C -->|"git push"| D
    D -->|"git pull"| A






Three things to notice, because each one causes a specific student disaster:

commit is local. Committing does not put your work on GitHub. You can commit all week on a plane and nobody sees a thing.
push is the only move that publishes. Until you push, your teammates cannot see your work — and if your laptop dies, it is gone.
pull is the only move that brings other people’s work to you. If you have not pulled today, you are working on yesterday’s version of the project.







Why is there a staging area at all?



So you can commit some of your changes and not others. You fixed a typo and half-rewrote the model; you can commit the typo fix on its own. Most of the time Claude will stage everything relevant and you will never think about it.

title: Part 1 — The four ideas
section: Idea 2: a commit is a labelled snapshot
text:
Idea 2: a commit is a labelled snapshot
A commit is the whole project at one moment, plus:

who made it
when
a message saying why

The history is a chain of these snapshots. This is the entire reason git can undo things: every previous state still exists.
The message is for a human — probably you, in five weeks, wondering why the model changed. "update", "fixes" and "asdf" are worthless. Good messages say why, because the what is already visible in the diff:






Good




Drop 3 participants with impossible ages — the export had -1 for missing









Useless




fixed data



This is genuinely something Claude does better than most humans, so let it.

title: Part 1 — The four ideas
section: Idea 3: a branch is a parallel line of work
text:
Idea 3: a branch is a parallel line of work
A branch lets you build something half-finished without breaking the version everyone else is using.





%%{init: {'gitGraph': {'rotateCommitLabel': false, 'showBranches': true}}}%%
gitGraph
    commit id: "setup"
    branch sex-table
    commit id: "your work"
    checkout main
    merge sex-table id: "PR #1"
    commit id: "next"






main is the branch that must always work. You do your work on a branch named after what you are doing, then you merge it back into main.
A Pull Request (PR) is a merge with a conversation attached: it happens on GitHub, your teammates can see exactly what changed, comment on it, and press Merge. In this course the rule is: you do not merge your own pull request. A teammate does. That single rule is the whole of code review.

title: Part 1 — The four ideas
section: Idea 4: a conflict means git refuses to guess
text:
Idea 4: a conflict means git refuses to guess
If you change lines 40–43 of report.qmd and your teammate changes the same lines, git cannot know which version is right. So it stops, puts both versions in the file surrounded by markers, and tells you to decide:
<<<<<<< HEAD
Treatment was associated with a lower score than control (adjusted
difference -5.23, 95% CI -7.53 to -2.94).
=======
In this simulated dataset the treatment arm scored about 5 points lower
than control after adjustment for age and sex.
>>>>>>> de43b31
Read it as: above ======= is mine, below is theirs.






A conflict is not an error, and it is not the AI’s decision



This is git protecting you. The alternative — a tool that silently picks one version — would lose your work without telling you.
And notice what the example above actually is: two people who each said something true that the other left out. The right answer is usually both, rewritten. Claude can delete the markers for you in a second; only your group knows what the paragraph is supposed to claim.

title: Part 1 — The four ideas
text:
The napkin check
Before you touch a computer, on paper, without looking:

Draw the four places and label the three moves between them.
You committed your work this morning but your teammate cannot see it. Which move did you forget?
Your teammate says “it works on my machine” and you cannot reproduce it. Which move did you forget?
In your own words: what is a merge conflict, and who resolves it?







Answers






push. 3. pull. 4. Two people changed the same lines; git refuses to choose; the humans who wrote them decide, then commit the decision.

title: Git for group work
text:
Your group project lives in files: R scripts, a Quarto report, maybe some data. Several of you will edit those files over several weeks. You need a way to do that without emailing zip files, without analysis_final_v3_ULO_REALLY_FINAL.R, and without silently overwriting each other’s work.
That is what git and GitHub are for. By the end of this tutorial your group will have:

one GitHub repository that everybody can read and write
a history of who changed what, when, and why
a way to work at the same time without destroying each other’s work
a main branch that always runs

title: Git for group work
section: The deal about AI doing the work
text:
The deal about AI doing the work
You will not memorise git commands. Claude Code will type them for you, and it is better at writing commit messages than you are.
But you do have to understand four ideas, because when things go wrong — and they will — the AI can fix the mechanics while only you can decide what is correct. When two of you have written different interpretations of the same result, no amount of AI can tell you which sentence your group means to publish.






The bar you have to clear



By the end of Part 1 you must be able to draw the four-places diagram from memory and explain what a merge conflict is. That is the whole theory requirement. Everything else you can delegate.

title: Git for group work
text:
What you will build
A small R project called penguin-clinic: simulated clinic data, three analysis scripts, and a shared Quarto report. It is deliberately structured so that each group member owns one file — and so that one section of the report is shared, to make you deal with a merge conflict on purpose, in a safe place, before it happens for real at 23:00 the night before a deadline.
A worked version of the finished repository, with all its history and its pull request, is here: github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic.

title: Git for group work
section: How to read the code blocks
text:
How to read the code blocks
Most steps are shown twice:






Say this to Claude Code




Commit my changes with a message explaining that I added the sex-stratified table.



# what it actually runs
git add R/02-describe.R
git commit -m "Add sex-stratified descriptives"
Read the prompt. Glance at the commands. Do not memorise the commands.

title: Part 5 — Group rules of the road
text: Put these in your project’s README and hold each other to them.
crumbs: Part 5 — Group rules of the road

title: Part 5 — Group rules of the road
text:
The seven rules

1. Pull before you start. Push when you stop.

The single habit that prevents most pain. Check RStudio’s Git pane arrows every time you sit down.

2. main must always run.

Anyone should be able to pull main and render the report. If you break it, fixing it is your only priority. Nobody can work on a broken base.

3. Work on a branch; a teammate merges your pull request.

Never merge your own. The five minutes a teammate spends reading your diff is the cheapest quality control available.

4. Own your files.

Put the ownership table in the README. Conflicts need two people in the same lines — so mostly, do not be there.

5. Commit small, commit often, say why.

One idea per commit. The message explains why, because the diff already shows what.

6. Never commit anything you would not email to a stranger.

No patient data, no passwords, no API keys, no .Renviron. Git never forgets: deleting a file later does not remove it from the history, and a pushed secret must be treated as burned. Get .gitignore right first.

7. Never git push --force on a shared branch.

It deletes your teammates’ commits. If you think you need it, ask.
crumbs: Part 5 — Group rules of the road

title: Part 5 — Group rules of the road
text:
Commit message shape
Short line saying what changed (under ~60 characters)

Then a blank line, then why — the reasoning, the alternative you rejected,
the thing that will not be obvious in six weeks.
Real example from this project:

Set up project skeleton for the git tutorial
The .gitignore excludes RStudio session state, rendered output and secrets, but deliberately keeps the 4 KB synthetic CSV so students see that “never commit data” is a judgement, not a rule.

title: Part 5 — Group rules of the road
section: A README that makes the group work
text:
A README that makes the group work
# Project title

One sentence on what this analyses.

## Who owns what
| File | Owner |
|------|-------|
| R/01-clean.R | A |
| R/02-describe.R | B |
| R/03-model.R | C |
| report.qmd, Interpretation | everyone |

## How to run it
Open the .Rproj in RStudio, then: quarto render report.qmd

## Where the data come from
Simulated by data-raw/00-simulate-data.R. No real people.
The ownership table is not bureaucracy. It is your conflict-avoidance mechanism written down.

title: Part 5 — Group rules of the road
section: What good looks like at the end of term
text:
What good looks like at the end of term

30–80 small commits, not 4 giant ones
messages a stranger could follow
every contribution went through a pull request someone else merged
main renders on any group member’s laptop
no data file over a megabyte, no secrets, ever
and when your report says a number, you can point at the commit that produced it

That last one is worth more than the version control. A project whose history you can walk is a project whose results you can defend.

title: Part 0 — One-time setup
text: Do this once per computer, before the session. Budget 20 minutes, and do it while you have decent internet.

title: Part 0 — One-time setup
text:
1. Install the four tools

macOSWindowsLinux (Debian/Ubuntu)


xcode-select --install       # installs git (and much else); skip if already done
brew install gh              # GitHub CLI
R and RStudio: download from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop (install R first, then RStudio).
No Homebrew? Get gh from cli.github.com.



Git — git-scm.com/download/win. Accept the defaults. This also installs Git Bash, a terminal where these commands work.
GitHub CLI — cli.github.com.
R then RStudio — posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop.







Note



Run the commands in this tutorial in Git Bash or in RStudio’s Terminal tab, not in PowerShell, unless you know what you are doing.




sudo apt update && sudo apt install git gh r-base
RStudio from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop.

title: Part 0 — One-time setup
text:
2. Make a GitHub account
github.com/signup. Use an email you will still have after you graduate. Turn on two-factor authentication when it asks — GitHub requires it and you will be forced to eventually anyway.






Pick a username you would put on a CV



Your GitHub profile is public and outlives the course. ulo-maivali ages better than xX_stats_destroyer_Xx.

title: Part 0 — One-time setup
text:
3. Log in from your computer
gh auth login -h github.com
Four prompts. Answer them like this:








Prompt
Answer
Why




Preferred protocol
HTTPS
Simpler than SSH keys; nothing to generate or lose


Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials?
Yes
This is what makes git push work without ever typing a password. Do not skip it.


How would you like to authenticate?
Login with a web browser
Creates a token with only the permissions you need


One-time code
press Return, paste the code in the browser, authorise










Do not paste a Personal Access Token unless you have to



The browser login mints a narrow, revocable token. A hand-made “classic” token often ends up with far more power than this course needs (organisation admin, for instance), and it sits on your laptop for years.

title: Part 0 — One-time setup
section: 4. Tell git who you are, and how to behave
text:
4. Tell git who you are, and how to behave
Four lines. Run them once; they apply to every project on this computer.
git config --global user.name "Your Actual Name"
git config --global user.email "the-email-you-used-for-github@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global pull.rebase false
Windows only, to stop line-ending noise in a mixed-OS group:
git config --global core.autocrlf true
Why each one matters:

user.name / user.email

Stamped into every commit you make, forever. On macOS git will silently fall back to your system account name if you skip this, so your commits may end up authored by “Admin”. Set it.

init.defaultBranch main

Git’s built-in default is still master on some versions; GitHub expects main. Mismatched names cause confusing push errors.

pull.rebase false

The most commonly skipped line, and it causes a hard failure. Without it, the first time your work and your teammate’s work diverge, git pull aborts with fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches. and eight lines of hints. false means “merge”, which is the honest, safe option — it never rewrites history you have already shared.

title: Part 0 — One-time setup
text:
5. Install the course plugin
Two commands, typed in Claude Code:
/plugin marketplace add ymaivali/claude-plugins
/plugin install git-workflow@ulo-plugins
Then start a new session. Skills load when a session starts, so they will not appear in the session you installed them in. That surprises everybody once.
This gives you two skills. You do not call them by name — you say what you want and the right one loads:







Say something like
What happens




“set up git for this project”
New repository: the .gitignore conversation, your commit identity, first commit, a GitHub repo, first push


“commit this”, “push it”, “am I behind?”, “open a PR”, “I have a conflict”
The everyday loop









It also installs a guard, and you should know what that means



The plugin adds a hook that sees every shell command Claude runs in your sessions, and blocks a short list of git commands that destroy work git cannot recover: --force pushes, remote branch deletion, reset --hard, clean -f.
It receives the text of the command and nothing else — no file contents, no environment variables, no credentials — and it sends nothing anywhere. It is about 90 lines of Python you can read, and it ships with a 53-case test suite so you can check that rather than take my word for it:
python3 ~/.claude/plugins/*/plugins/git-workflow/hooks/git-guard-test.py
It restrains Claude, not you: you can always run the command yourself in your own terminal. Full detail, including how to install the skills without the guard, is in the plugin’s README.

title: Part 0 — One-time setup
text:
6. Check it worked
git --version
gh auth status
git config --global --list | grep -E "user|branch|rebase"
R --version
python3 --version
You want: a git version, ✓ Logged in to github.com account <you>, your four config lines, and an R version. If gh auth status says your token is invalid, run gh auth login again.






Stuck?



Paste the entire error message into Claude Code and say “this happened while setting up git, what do I do?”. Pasting the whole message including the hints matters — the hints usually contain the answer.
